v.q: Where do objects and where do local primitive variables normally live in the JVM?
o: Objects on the heap; locals on the thread's stack
Objects on the stack; locals on the heap
Both objects and locals on the heap
Both objects and locals on the stack
v.w: Each thread has its own stack of frames. The heap is shared. References on the stack point to objects on the heap.

v.q: Which statement about heap and stack is NOT true?
o: Local variables of a method live on the heap
Objects live on the heap
Each thread has its own stack
A local reference points to a heap object
v.w: Locals and call frames live on the thread stack. Only the objects they refer to are on the heap.

v.q: Thread A sets `ready = true` (a plain field) and thread B loops `while(!ready)`. Why might B never stop?
o: Without synchronisation B may keep reading a cached value
Booleans cannot be shared between two threads
The JVM kills any thread that spins in a loop
The write is always delayed by about a second
v.w: The Java Memory Model gives no visibility guarantee for plain fields. Mark the field `volatile` or use a proper synchroniser.

v.q: Which change makes the loop while(!ready) reliably stop when another thread sets ready?
o: Declare ready as volatile
Declare ready as private
Add an empty loop body comment
Make ready a local variable
v.w: Volatile guarantees that the write becomes visible to the reading thread.

v.q: What does a happens-before relationship guarantee?
o: Actions in one thread are visible and ordered for another
The first action runs earlier by the wall clock
Both actions run on the same CPU core
The second action is guaranteed not to fail
v.w: Examples: unlock happens-before a later lock of the same monitor; a volatile write happens-before a later read of it; `Thread.start()` happens-before the thread's actions.

v.q: Which action creates a happens-before edge between two threads?
o: Releasing and then acquiring the same lock
Calling the two methods in the same class
Printing a message
Using the same variable name
v.w: Unlock followed by lock on the same monitor orders and publishes the earlier writes. Volatile and Thread.start do the same.

v.q: Which statement about `final` fields is correct for safe publication?
o: Other threads see correctly initialised final fields after construction
Final fields can still be changed by using `volatile`
Final fields are stored outside the heap
Final fields are checked only at compile time
v.w: The JMM gives final fields special initialisation safety, provided `this` does not escape the constructor.

v.q: Which statement about final fields is NOT true?
o: A final field can be changed later with volatile
They are safely visible after construction
They cannot be reassigned after construction
They help build immutable objects
v.w: Volatile and final are different. A final field cannot be reassigned.

v.q: What is Metaspace used for in modern JVMs?
o: Class metadata, held in native memory
The stack frames of every thread
Interned strings only, nothing else
Young-generation objects awaiting collection
v.w: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8. It grows in native memory and can leak through class loader leaks.

v.q: Which memory area is NOT part of the heap in a modern JVM?
o: Metaspace
Young generation
Old generation
Survivor space
v.w: Metaspace holds class metadata in native memory, outside the heap.

v.q: A recursive method has no base case. Which error do you get?
o: `StackOverflowError`
`OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`
`ClassCastException`
`ConcurrentModificationException`
v.w: Each call adds a stack frame. Deep recursion exhausts the thread stack. Heap exhaustion gives `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.

v.q: Which of these is NOT a result of a recursive method with no base case?
o: ClassCastException
StackOverflowError
A very deep stack of frames
A thread that never returns
v.w: Deep recursion overflows the stack. ClassCastException comes from a wrong cast and has nothing to do with depth.

v.q: What can the JVM and CPU do to code that has no synchronisation?
o: Reorder independent reads and writes if one thread sees no change
Never change the order of any statements
Run each statement at most once per second
Convert every field into a volatile field
v.w: Reordering is legal within a thread's own view. Synchronisation (volatile, locks) establishes the ordering other threads can rely on.

v.q: Which statement about instruction reordering is NOT true?
o: It can never be seen from another thread
The compiler may reorder independent actions
The CPU may reorder independent actions
Synchronisation restricts it
v.w: Other threads can see reordered effects unless a happens-before edge prevents it.

v.q: Why is double-checked locking for a lazy singleton only correct with a `volatile` field?
o: Another thread could see a reference to a partly built object
Volatile makes the lock itself run faster
Without it the class cannot be loaded
Volatile stops the object being garbage collected
v.w: The reference can become visible before the constructor's writes. A volatile write prevents that reordering.

v.q: What does volatile guarantee on the instance field of a double-checked singleton?
o: A fully built object when the reference is seen
That only one instance is ever created
That the constructor runs faster
That the instance is never garbage collected
v.w: Volatile forbids publishing the reference before the construction writes, so no thread sees a half-built object.
